title: The Catawba and the northern war parties
summary: For half a century after the Great Peace of 1701, Iroquois and Shawnee war parties crossed the mountains to strike the Catawba of the Carolina Piedmont, along paths that ran beside Kentucky.
bodyMarkdown:
The Catawba never lived in Kentucky. For much of the eighteenth century, though, they were the reason war parties from the north crossed the mountains, and some of the paths those parties walked ran through or beside the Kentucky country.

## People of the river

The [Catawba](https://grokipedia.com/page/Catawba_people) are a Siouan-speaking people whose ancestors lived for thousands of years along the Catawba River in the Piedmont of the present Carolinas. A Spanish expedition recorded them there in 1567. In the 1700s they were a confederation of towns, allied with South Carolina, and known as hard fighters. The Haudenosaunee called them [Toderichroone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catawba_people); the French called them Têtes plates, the Flatheads.

## War turned south

Northern war parties were already striking southern nations by the 1670s. In August 1701 the [Great Peace of Montreal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Peace_of_Montreal) ended the long wars between the Five Nations Iroquois, New France, and the Native nations of the Great Lakes. Peace in the north did not end the young men’s need for war honors, or the grief of families who wanted captives to replace their dead. As [one study of these southern wars](https://archipel.uqam.ca/10139/) shows, the raids now turned south against the Cherokee, the Chickasaw, and above all the Catawba, and French officials encouraged them.

Parties of two to forty warriors walked hundreds of miles to strike and carry home prisoners.

The Catawba struck back, and in the 1720s and 1730s their warriors chased Lenape raiders north across the Potomac. Colonial governors, who counted both sides as allies, tried again and again to stop it. In 1717, during peace talks near Virginia’s Fort Christanna, a [Seneca party attacked unarmed Catawbas](https://blogs.charleston.edu/colonial-carolina/the-committee-of-conference-upon-indian-affairs-report-may-1751/), killing five. Councils at Albany in 1721 and at Lancaster in 1744 tried to settle the feud.

In 1751 the Catawba leader Haigler traveled to Albany to make peace with the Six Nations, but the cease-fire held only briefly; within two years Iroquois warriors were raiding again.

## The Kentucky road

Some of that traffic moved through the Kentucky country. The [great warpath system](https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Indian_Warpath) of the backcountry tied the northern nations to the Catawba and Cherokee towns. One branch crossed eastern Kentucky to Cumberland Gap along the trail the Shawnee called [Athiamiowee](/stories/athiamiowee-the-warriors-path-through-kentucky/). By the 1750s English speakers knew that trail as the Warriors’ Path.

The Shawnee were Catawba enemies too. In 1753 South Carolina jailed six Shawnee warriors on their way to attack the Catawba. The best known of them, [Itawachcomequa, called The Pride](https://read.dukeupress.edu/ethnohistory/article-abstract/53/4/657/8615/Shawnee-Origins-of-Their-Seven-Years-War), died in confinement. His people answered with a declaration of war against the British colonies in 1754, a quarrel that would run through the Ohio Valley for decades.

## What came after

Smallpox struck the Catawba in 1738 and again in 1759, when it [killed nearly half of them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catawba_people). In 1763 a small Shawnee party killed Haigler near his own town, and that same year South Carolina confirmed a Catawba reservation of 144,000 acres. The Catawba Nation endured. Its federal recognition came in 1941, was terminated in 1959, and was restored in 1993, and its reservation near Rock Hill, South Carolina, keeps alive a pottery tradition thousands of years old.

These events took place outside Kentucky, so this story has no Kentucky map pin.
